text: A worn runway look centered on a glossy heat-sealed leather jacket sculpted into a bell. The leather reads smooth and sealed rather than matte, with a flared body that widens away from the torso and a crafted, molded volume through the hem. It is shown in the sunny yellow-and-red register of the collection's opening color note. The jacket is the identifying garment: a leather-house piece pushed into a bell-shaped outer shell, worn as a single high-craft layer over the body rather than as a flat tailored blazer.

A worn runway dress built from multiple draped scarf layers. The seams are left with their allowances turned outward, so each join becomes a cascade of ruffles running through the drape. The body is covered by overlapping scarf panels rather than a single cut of cloth, and the ruffled seam edges mark the path of the layers from the shoulder area down the length of the dress. The result is a fluid, layered garment whose identity is the exposed seam-allowance ruffle, not a plain slip dress.

A worn runway look that takes the jeans archetype and remakes it in shredded leather. The leg keeps a jeans-like cut, but the surface is leather broken into shreds rather than denim twill. The shredding is the identifying field: strips and opened edges run along the leg, so the garment reads as sportswear passed through leather craft. It is worn on the body as the lower half of the look, with the shredded leather leg as the point that must stay recognizable.

A worn button-down shirt made of leather that has been hand-pleated and spray-painted. The shirt keeps a button-down front, but the leather is broken into fine hand pleats and the surface carries spray-painted color over the pleats. The identity is that crafted leather shirting: pleat ridges catching paint, worn as an upper garment in place of a cloth button-down. The pleated, painted leather field has to remain visible across the front and sleeves.

A worn tank or tee whose cloth is leather yarn shot through with wire. The wire holds the leather strands into a crinkled, irregular shape, so the top does not hang like jersey. It is worn close to the torso as a simple tank or T-shirt silhouette, but the surface buckles and crisps where the wire runs through the leather yarn. That crinkled leather-yarn field is the identifying surface and should not be smoothed into ordinary knit.

A worn dress made from a 3-D printed fabric given the pile of velvet, described as a towel dress. The body is covered in a soft piled surface that reads like toweling or velvet rather than a flat weave, and the cloth itself is a printed construction. The dress is worn as one garment, with that piled, towel-like field as its identity from the upper body through the skirt. The pile has to stay visible; it is not a smooth satin column.

A worn look opened by a pure, stark cotton tunic with a stand collar, paired with stockings whose tops release a cascade of silk fringe. The tunic is simple and collar-standing, cut as a short-coat-like cotton layer. Below it, silk fringe falls from the stocking tops and moves against the leg. The contrast is the identifying pair: a plain stand-collar cotton tunic above, and the cascading silk fringe at the stocking line. Both have to remain readable on the body.

A worn body-conscious look in seamless silk knit shaped into taut arches. The knit is held in place at the wrists and hooked into the heels of the shoes, so the garment is tensioned from hand to foot rather than ending in a free hem. The silk knit lies close to the body, seamless, with the arched spans as the silhouette. The identity is that continuous pulled knit: wrist anchors, heel hooks, and the arched line between them.

A worn fit-and-flare knit dress in the house's close-bodied knit, with the skirt cut on an angle instead of finished as a flounce. The bodice stays fitted and the skirt flares, but the hem and flare are angled rather than a rounded ruffle. It is worn as one knit garment on the body. The identifying change is that angled skirt: the flare has a slanted edge, not a flounced Alaïa hem.

A worn hybrid lower garment: skirt-pants left open at the sides. The piece reads as both a skirt and a pant, with the side openings exposing the construction so the two forms are visible at once. It is worn on the body, the open sides marking a continuous edge from hip toward the hem. The identity is that open-sided skirt-pant, not a closed trouser and not a closed skirt.

A worn one-piece hybrid: a backless turtleneck continued into sweater-leggings. The neck is a turtleneck, the back is open, and the knit does not stop at the hip; it continues down the legs as leggings. It is worn as a single knitted body, with the open back and the legging extension both visible. The identity is that backless turtleneck-to-legging knit, not a separate sweater over separate tights.

A worn coat enlarged into a soft sculpture of twisting fringe layers. The coat is huge and glamorous, its body built from layers of fringe that twist around the silhouette rather than a flat tailored cloth. It is worn over the body as an outer wrap, with the twisting fringe making both the volume and the surface. The identity is that fringed, twisting coat-sculpture; the fringe layers have to stay readable as the coat itself.

A worn ball skirt in duchess satin, cut stately and vaguely panniered. The satin skirt extends at the sides in a softened eighteenth-century width, with the duchess satin holding a formal, structured flare. It is worn as the lower half of the look, the wide satin pannier shape as the identifying silhouette. The skirt should keep that side-extended satin volume rather than falling as a narrow column.

A worn sweeping coat with the abstract air of a North African burnous, shown with the collection's easier shapes beside edge-to-edge jackets. The coat wraps and sweeps, loose rather than hourglass, with an enveloping outer line. It is worn open enough for the wrap to read, the long sweep of cloth as the silhouette. The identity is that burnous-like sweeping coat, not a fitted trench and not the fringe sculpture coat.

A worn look built as a vintage silk shantung pajama ensemble with a cashmere sweater vest. The pajama is silk shantung, so the surface has that dry, crisp sheen, cut as a matching relaxed set. The cashmere vest sits over it as a softer knit layer. Low pumps are worn with the pajama hem. The identity is the shantung pajama left visible under the cashmere vest, not a tailored suit and not a bare evening dress.

A worn yellow cape cut as sturdy as a Mackintosh. The cloth holds a firm, weather-coat body rather than a fluttering chiffon wrap, and the color is a clear yellow. It is worn over the shoulders as a cape, the solid yellow shell making one continuous outer shape. The identity is that jaunty, structured yellow cape; it should not collapse into a soft scarf or a tailored yellow blazer.

A worn cashmere coat with the ease of a robe. The coat is cashmere, soft in the hand, and cut with a robe-like looseness rather than a sharp shoulder or a belted trench waist. It is worn as an outer layer that hangs with that dressing-gown ease, the cashmere surface continuous from shoulder to hem. The identity is the robe-easy cashmere coat, not a structured overcoat and not the yellow cape.

A worn look in which white jersey underpinnings, slubbed like cloth that has been washed many times, are used as the visible outfit rather than hidden underwear. Inside and outside clothes are worn as one layered look, finished with heels. The jersey is white and slightly irregular from the slub, and more than one layer is readable on the body. The identity is that washed white jersey stack, dressed up by the heels, not a formal gown placed over invisible underwear.

A worn tailored look pared back to clean lines, then interrupted by pebble-shaped pockets and a curved waistband. The tailoring itself is reduced, without the house's usual gold hardware, and the off-kilter details sit on that quiet cloth: pockets rounded like pebbles, a waistband that curves instead of running straight. It is worn as a tailored garment on the body. The identity is those pebble pockets and the curved waistband on otherwise restrained tailoring.

A worn leather shirt punched with oversized holes. The shirt is leather, and the holes are large enough to read as a repeated opening through the material rather than small perforations. It is worn on the torso as a shirt, with the punched field visible across the leather. The identity is that hole-punched leather shirt; the openings have to stay part of the surface, not be filled back in as solid leather.

A worn evening gown in the 1930s manner: glossy satin panels floating on a sheer base, with chain straps. The satin does not make a solid opaque dress; panels of gloss sit on sheer ground so both layers are visible, and the straps are chains. It is worn on the body, the sheer base and the satin panels moving together, the chains marking the shoulder line. The identity is that satin-on-sheer panel gown with chain straps, not a fully lined column and not a corseted hourglass.
